extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IPR practitioners, patent examiners, and judges evaluating patent obviousness (particularly in pharmaceutical/biotech cases)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria used by an adjudicative body (PTAB/Fed. Cir. context) to evaluate obviousness of patent claims, with emphasis on pharmaceuticals (combination therapies), prior art weight, motivation to combine, expectation of success, and secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in IPR obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner must establish unpatentability of the challenged claims by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board states that, after reviewing the record, the Petitioner established by a preponderance of the evidence that the challenged claims are unpatentable. Use this standard when weighing documentary and expert evidence in IPR proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze prior art as a whole (cannot attack references only individually)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-obviousness cannot be established by attacking references individually where the patentability challenge is based upon the teachings of a combination of references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Keller and In re Fulton: consider the totality of teachings across references and the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) when assessing motivation to combine or predictability. Do not dismiss a combination rejection because each reference alone lacks a particular teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a reason an ordinary artisan would have been motivated to combine the prior art teachings (references) to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation may come from explicit statements in references (e.g., Baselga ’96 specifically teaching paclitaxel as a chemotherapeutic to combine with rhuMAb HER2), preclinical data suggesting potentiation/synergy, or the general knowledge of POSITA. Consider contemporaneous statements, citations, and clinical-trial plans as evidence of motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference that discourages or warns against the claimed combination may undermine motivation to combine, i.e., it 'teaches away.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the prior art's discouragement is general or specific to the experimental conditions (e.g., Yu's in vitro warning about Taxol in HER2-overexpressing cells was judged not to teach away when it was limited to in vitro conditions and contradicted by in vivo data and other clinical evidence). Consider scope, model differences, and whether a POSITA would generalize the warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: To show obviousness, petitioner must demonstrate a POSITA would have had a reasonable expectation of success in achieving the claimed result (e.g., clinical efficacy or safety).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation need only be reasonable, not absolute. Use relevant prior art (preclinical and clinical), known safety information, and contemporaneous regulatory actions (e.g., FDA acceptance of trials) to evaluate whether a reasonable expectation existed. Compare appropriate endpoints (e.g., time to progression) using the correct baseline (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try / obviousness of attempting combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether it would have been 'obvious to try' a particular combination can inform obviousness, but is not required where prior art explicitly suggests the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether there were finite identified options, a reasonable expectation of success, and whether the prior art explicitly suggested trying the combination. The Board did not resolve 'obvious to try' here because the prior art expressly suggested the combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) and nexus requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia such as long-felt but unmet need, praise, unexpected results, and commercial success may support nonobviousness, but their probative weight requires establishing a nexus between the evidence and the novel aspects of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply In re Huai-Hung Kao: if the objective evidence results from something other than what is both claimed and novel, there is no nexus. Examples: commercial success must be tied to the claimed features; unexpected results must be attributable to the claimed invention rather than other causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight given to abstracts and preclinical disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts and preliminary preclinical disclosures can be persuasive prior art and may motivate a POSITA to act, particularly when authored by leading practitioners and later cited by peer-reviewed literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically discount abstracts because they are preliminary. Consider: (1) whether the patent or prosecution relied on abstracts, (2) whether authors are credible and collaborative with practitioners, (3) whether later literature cited the abstract with approval, and (4) expert testimony about how POSITAs treat abstracts in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive value of animal models and in vitro studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether preclinical in vivo (xenograft) or in vitro data would have led a POSITA to expect similar clinical results; not all models are equivalent in predictive value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider model type (ectopic vs orthotopic), cell line selection (natural overexpression vs transfected), dose/schedule information, and contemporaneous practice (e.g., widespread use of ectopic xenograft models). Lack of dose or overexpression detail may reduce the force of a reference. Corroboration by other studies and subsequent citations increases persuasive weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate baseline for claimed clinical endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing claims reciting clinical outcomes (e.g., 'an amount effective to extend the time to disease progression'), identify the proper comparison baseline (e.g., no treatment or a specific comparator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board noted that the proper analysis of 'extend the time to disease progression' is to compare the claimed combination to no treatment in some contexts, and also evaluated comparisons to paclitaxel alone when relevant. Ensure claim construction and the record determine the correct comparator.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDA regulatory actions and submissions are relevant evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory submissions and the FDA's acceptance of trial rationale may be relevant to motivation and reasonable expectation of success in an obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent owner proposed clinical trials to the FDA based on the same prior-art rationale, and the FDA found the trial acceptable, that can support that POSITAs would have considered the combination reasonable and safe to try. Use FDA-related contemporaneous documents as corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpredictability does not preclude obviousness if reasonable probability exists
rubrics_metrics.description: The inherent unpredictability of the pharmaceutical arts does not, by itself, avoid an obviousness finding so long as there was a reasonable probability (reasonable expectation) of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Pfizer and Allergan: courts require only a reasonable probability of success. Consider overall prior art and known safety/efficacy information rather than focusing solely on industry failure rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of known combinations does not defeat obviousness for same purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that prior art discloses many effective combinations does not render any particular combination less obvious when the claimed composition is used for the identical purpose taught by the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Merck v. Biocraft: if prior art expressly teaches combining the types of components for the same purpose, selecting one known component among many does not necessarily confer nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment from perspective of POSITA; inventor development history largely irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability is assessed from the hypothetical person of ordinary skill in the art; how the inventor developed the claimed invention is not material to the objective obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on what a POSITA would have known and done at the relevant time. Inventor's internal development difficulties or colleague resistance do not control the legal obviousness inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary value of comparative numerical data (e.g., response rates, median TTP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical results in prior art (e.g., % response, median time to progression) can be used to support expectation of clinical improvement or to show a claimed benefit relative to known treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contemporaneous clinical data and drug labeling (e.g., TAXOL PDR median TTP) to compare to reported results in the art (e.g., Baselga ’96 reporting 5.1 months TTP). Recognize surrogate endpoints (response rate) were often used as proxies for endpoints like TTP in early-phase trials; weigh accordingly.
